Dearth
DURTH
noun
From dear in its old English sense of costly or scarce, with the abstract ending -th; hence dearness of victuals, scarcity of bread — the state in which food is present but priced beyond the poor man’s reach.

Biblical Definition

Dearth is scarcity of food and the dearness of bread that follows it — famine considered from the side of the market and the empty purse. The Authorized Version uses it where corn is short and men must mortgage to eat. It falls upon the whole known world in Joseph’s day: “And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread” (Gen 41:54) — and that last clause is the whole doctrine of providence in eight words. God had sent a man before them, sold for a servant, to preserve life by a great deliverance; the dearth that emptied every other granary filled the one God had prepared. Stephen rehearses it before the council as the hinge of the patriarchal history (Act 7:11). Elisha meets a dearth in Gilgal and turns death in the pot into food for the sons of the prophets (2Ki 4:38). Nehemiah’s poor mortgage their lands and vineyards because of the dearth, and the reformer’s anger falls not on the weather but on the usurers who profited by it (Neh 5:3). And Agabus foretells a dearth throughout all the world, which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar (Act 11:28) — whereupon the church at Antioch immediately sent relief to the brethren in Judaea.

Webster 1828 Definition

Scarcity of food and consequent dearness of provisions; in Scripture an appointed providence that both humbles nations and reveals whether mercy is in God’s people.

expand to see more

DEARTH, scarcity; particularly a scarcity of provisions, and the high price which attends it; want of corn.

From dear, costly, scarce; the old English sense survives in speaking of a dearth of anything.

Distinguished in usage from famine chiefly by emphasis: famine names the want, dearth names the dearness.

Gen 41:54 and Act 7:11 apply it to the seven years foretold to Pharaoh and administered by Joseph.

Act 11:28 records the dearth foretold by Agabus in the reign of Claudius Caesar.

Key Scripture

Gen 41:54 — "And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread."

Act 7:11 — "Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance."

2Ki 4:38 — "And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets."

Act 11:28 — "And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar."

Modern Corruption

Scarcity is treated as a purely economic event with no Governor above it and no duty of mercy within it — a problem for policy rather than an occasion for providence and alms.

expand to see more

The common misuse of dearth is to hand it over entirely to management. Grain fails, prices rise, and the whole account is told in mechanisms — supply, harvest yields, hoarding, tariff — as though there were no throne above the field. Scripture tells the mechanisms too. It records Joseph’s twenty-per-cent levy in the years of plenty, his storehouses, his rationing, his land policy; the Bible is not squeamish about administration. But it insists the mechanism is the servant of a purpose: God sent a dreamer to Egypt in chains seventeen years before the first thin ear appeared, and the granary that fed the nations was built by a providence that Joseph’s brothers meant for evil and God meant unto good. Strip out that Governor and dearth becomes either blind misfortune or somebody’s fault, and the two answers between them exhaust the modern imagination. Scripture has a third: a Father who ordains scarcity and who has already, before the scarcity, prepared bread for those He means to keep.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that dearth tests the church’s bowels of mercy. Notice what happens the moment Agabus prophesies: the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, and sent it by Barnabas and Saul. No debate, no committee — a prophecy of hunger produced a collection. Nehemiah shows the negative pattern: when the dearth came, some in Judah used it to take their brethren’s fields in pledge, and Nehemiah confronted them until they restored what they had taken. Scarcity does not create character; it publishes it. The same want that turned some men into usurers turned others into the mercy of God with skin on. And behind both stands the Lord who fed Israel with manna, who multiplied loaves on a hillside, and who taught His people to pray daily for bread — that they might learn, in a year of dearth, whose hand had been feeding them all along in the years of plenty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Scarcity of bread and dearness of price; the providence that emptied every granary but the one God had prepared beforehand.

expand to see more

Dearth — from dear, costly or scarce, with the abstract suffix -th.

Renders Hebrew ra‘ab (hunger, famine) and Greek limos in the New Testament.

Gen 41:54 — “the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.”

2Ki 4:38 sets a dearth at Gilgal, where Elisha heals the poisoned pottage.

Act 11:28 — Agabus foretells the dearth under Claudius; Antioch answers it with alms.

Usage

"Dearth names the dearness of bread, famine the want of it — the same providence seen from the purse."

"God prepared the granary before He sent the scarcity; Joseph went down in chains seventeen years early."

"A prophecy of dearth produced a collection at Antioch — scarcity publishes what a church is made of."
